title: The Tragedy of Nikole Hannah-Jones https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2026/09/the-tragedy-of-nikole-hannah-jones.html
author: Alex Tabarrok
summary: Economist Alex Tabarrok acknowledges the courage of Nikole Hannah-Jones's account of her daughter's schooling, calling it raw and true about her personal choices but mostly false about the larger story. He argues that the failures she documents are failures of management and accountability, not funding, noting that New York City spends over $40,000 per pupil and P.S. 307 over $52,000. Tabarrok says ideology blinded her to the meaning of high grades paired with failing standardized test scores, which most parents would read as proof the classes were a lie. He finds the essay an excellent demonstration of why voice fails, even a powerful voice, without the threat of exit. He ends with an Ayn Rand reference and the point that a child may not deserve more than other children in the abstract but is entitled to expect more from her own parent.
points: Tabarrok argues within-state funding gaps by race or income have not been large for decades.
High class grades combined with failed standardized tests signaled that Najya's classes were not teaching her.
Najya's collapse in confidence and new test anxiety show the costs of social promotion.
He reads the essay as a case study in why voice fails without a credible threat of exit.
Hannah-Jones invoked the history of school integration to justify keeping her child in a segregated school.
quotes: The piece is raw and true when talking about her personal choices, but the larger story in which NHJ embeds her personal history is mostly false. The problem isn’t funding. The failures she documents are failures of management and accountability, not lack of resources.
NHJ has reckoned with her failing her own child but she has not yet reckoned with the failure of her entire educational philosophy.
NHJ’s daughter earns high grades in her math classes but she fails standardized tests. Most parents, especially conservatives, know what that means. The classes are a lie.
Ironically, NHJ invokes the heroic history of Black Americans integrating schools to justify keeping her own child in a segregated one. Painful.
But in the end she has written a great piece on why voice fails–even a powerful voice–in the absence of the threat of exit.
Nearly a decade later, Najya reminded her that in the abstract your child may not deserve more than other children, but she is nevertheless entitled to expect more from you.
